content: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a complex and diverse group of conditions characterized by elevated pulmonary artery pressure. If left untreated, it can lead to right-heart failure and death. PH is classified into five groups by the World Health Organization (WHO): Group 1 includes pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH); Group 2 involves PH due to left-heart disease (PH-LHD); Group 3 is associated with lung diseases or hypoxia; Group 4 is caused by chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH); and Group 5 includes cases with unclear or multifactorial mechanisms, such as hematological, systemic, or metabolic disorders. Phosphodiesterase type 5 (PDE5) inhibitors work by promoting vasodilation and inhibiting cellular proliferation. The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy of PDE5 inhibitors in treating pulmonary hypertension in both adults and children. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, CINAHL, and Web of Science, up to September 26, 2018. Additional sources, such as review articles, clinical trial registries, and reference lists, were also examined. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PDE5 inhibitors to placebo or other PAH-specific therapies for at least 12 weeks were included. Separate analyses were performed for each PH group. The primary outcomes assessed were changes in WHO functional class, six-minute walk distance (6MWD), and mortality. Secondary outcomes included hemodynamic parameters, quality of life, dyspnea, clinical worsening (e.g., hospitalization or need for intervention), and adverse events. Meta-analyses and subgroup analyses were conducted when appropriate, and the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. A total of 36 studies involving 2,999 participants with various forms of pulmonary hypertension were included in the final review. The average trial duration was 14 weeks, with some extending up to 12 months. Two trials specifically included children. Nineteen trials focused on Group 1 PAH participants. In this group, treatment with PDE5 inhibitors significantly improved WHO functional class (odds ratio [OR] 8.59, 95% confidence interval [CI] 3.95 to 18.72; 4 trials, 282 participants), increased 6MWD by 48 meters (95% CI 40 to 56; 8 trials, 880 participants), and reduced mortality by 22% over a mean duration of 14 weeks (95% CI 0.07 to 0.68; 8 trials, 1,119 participants). The number needed to treat (NNT) to prevent one additional death was 32 participants. However, PDE5 inhibitors were associated with an increased risk of adverse events, including headache (OR 1.97, 95% CI 1.33 to 2.92; 5 trials, 848 participants), gastrointestinal upset (OR 1.63, 95% CI 1.07 to 2.48; 5 trials, 848 participants), flushing (OR 4.12, 95% CI 1.83 to 9.26; 3 trials, 748 participants), and musculoskeletal pain (OR 2.52, 95% CI 1.59 to 3.99; 4 trials, 792 participants). Data comparing PDE5 inhibitors to placebo in combination with other PAH-specific therapies were limited due to the small number of trials. Participants receiving PDE5 inhibitors in combination therapy walked 19.66 meters further in six minutes (95% CI 9 to 30; 4 trials, 509 participants) compared to placebo (moderate-certainty evidence). Limited trials directly compared PDE5 inhibitors to other PAH-specific therapies, such as endothelin receptor antagonists (ERAs). In these comparisons, participants on PDE5 inhibitors walked 49 meters further than those on ERAs (95% CI 4 to 95; 2 trials, 36 participants), but the evidence was of low certainty. There was no significant difference in WHO functional class or mortality between the two treatments. In PH secondary to left-heart disease (PH-LHD), five trials compared PDE5 inhibitors to placebo. The quality of evidence was low due to imprecision and inconsistency across trials. In this group, PDE5 inhibitors were associated with reduced odds of improvement in WHO functional class compared to placebo (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.32 to 0.87; 3 trials, 285 participants). However, participants on PDE5 inhibitors walked 34 meters further than those on placebo (95% CI 23 to 46; 3 trials, 284 participants). There was no evidence of a difference in mortality. For PH secondary to lung disease or hypoxia, mostly in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), five trials compared PDE5 inhibitors to placebo. The evidence was of low quality due to imprecision and inconsistency. PDE5 inhibitors led to a modest improvement of 27 meters in 6MWD compared to placebo. There was no evidence of worsening hypoxia with PDE5 inhibitors, although the data were limited. In chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH), three studies compared PDE5 inhibitors to placebo or other PAH-specific therapies. No significant differences were observed in any outcomes. The quality of evidence was low due to imprecision and heterogeneity across trials. In conclusion, PDE5 inhibitors demonstrate clear benefits in Group 1 PAH, with sildenafil, tadalafil, and vardenafil all showing efficacy. Clinicians should consider the side-effect profiles of these drugs when prescribing. While there is some evidence of benefit in PH-LHD, the data are limited and suggest potential harm in cases of valvular heart disease. There is no clear benefit for PDE5 inhibitors in PH secondary to lung disease or CTEPH. Further research is needed to better understand the mechanisms of PH-LHD and to identify which subsets of patients may benefit from PDE5 inhibitors. Future trials should be adequately powered, include long-term follow-up, and assess invasive hemodynamic data, WHO functional class, 6MWD, and clinical worsening.
